sessions.title: I Lift Up My Eyes: The Songs of Ascent and the Long Climb
sessions.aim: To hear the Songs of Ascent as the songs of pilgrims on the road to Jerusalem, to take worship as a long and repeated climb rather than a single high moment, and to see how the whole Psalter gathers into praise that has passed through everything this study has walked.
sessions.summary:
The pilgrims who first sang the Songs of Ascent weren't on a spiritual high. They were on a long, dusty, uphill road to Jerusalem for the festivals, and these songs were what they sang to keep walking. Psalms 120 to 134 picture worship as it usually is: a repeated climb, not a permanent summit.

The collection moves like a road. Psalm 120 starts in distress, far from home. Psalm 121 lifts its eyes to the hills and finds help. The songs climb through trust, rescue, repentance and rest until Psalm 134, where servants in the temple bless God by night. Many of us long for the mountaintop, the felt nearness of God, and that longing is good. But a faith that counts only the highs as worship will judge the long road a failure, and the pilgrims sang on the road.

Then the turn that gathers the whole study. The Psalter ends in praise, but only after Psalm 88 and Psalm 137 and every how-long. We don't skip to the praise; we climb to it. And the God we climb toward has already come down the road to meet us.

keyScripture.why: "I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come? My help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth" (Psalm 121:1-2). A traveler on a long road looks past the hills, where danger lay, to the God who made them. Worship is the deliberate lifting of the eyes on an ordinary climb.

discussion.q: These psalms were walking songs, sung by tired families on the road to Jerusalem. How does it change them to hear them that way rather than as songs for a mountaintop moment?
discussion.behind: Move worship from the summit to the road. Most people picture worship as the intense moment, and these were sung by families climbing a literal hill for days. Help the room feel that most of worship is the walking: the repeated turning toward God on ordinary days.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 121. For a traveler, the hills were where danger lay. Where do you tend to look for help when you're in trouble, and what would it mean to look past that to the one who made it?
discussion.behind: Press on where the eyes go. Under pressure, most of us look to ourselves or our circumstances. The psalmist looks straight at the danger and past it to its Maker. Ask for specific places people look first.

discussion.q: Some people say worship should be the mountaintop, the felt nearness of God, and that a faith without those highs is just going through the motions. What's right in that hunger, and where does it mislead?
discussion.behind: The longing to feel God's nearness is good and shouldn't be despised. But if only the highs count, the long ordinary road will feel like failure, and the pilgrims sang on exactly that road. Help the room value the mountaintop without making it the only place worship happens.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 130:1-5 and Psalm 131. Even on the way up, the pilgrims cry from the depths and then quiet their souls "like a weaned child." What does it mean that repentance and rest are part of the climb?
discussion.behind: The road to the house of God still passes through the depths. Repentance isn't a detour from worship; it's part of the climb. And near the top the psalmist stops striving. Help the room see that the climb leads to rest in God, not to spiritual achievement.

discussion.q: Looking back over these five weeks, from lament to rage to trust to this long climb, how has walking the whole road changed what praise means to you?
discussion.behind: Gather the study. The praise at the end of the Psalter is earned, reached through everything the sessions have covered. Let people answer in their own words. End on worship and weight, not a tidy summary.

objections.objection: If worship is mostly the long boring climb and not the mountaintop, why bother? The point of faith is to experience God. A religion of just turning up and going through the motions on ordinary days sounds dead.
objections.response: The hunger in that is real. Longing to experience God is good, God isn't against it, and the mountaintop moments, when they come, are gifts to receive with joy. But look at the assumption underneath: that only the felt highs count as real worship and everything else is going through the motions. That assumption will wreck a life of faith. The pilgrims sang these songs on the road, tired and dusty and far from the summit, and their singing wasn't empty. It was worship, the deliberate turning of the heart toward God on an ordinary uphill day. Most of a real life with God is lived on that road, and a faith that can only worship on the peak will fall silent for the long stretches in between, which is most of the time. The faithful step taken when nothing is felt isn't lesser worship. It's the substance of it. The mountaintop is the gift, not the wage.

objections.objection: The Psalter ends in all that praise, which feels like the Bible papering over everything hard it said earlier. After Psalm 88 and Psalm 137, five psalms of hallelujah seem to take it all back.
objections.response: That's a serious worry, because a praise that erased the lament would betray everything the Psalter dared to say. But look at where the praise sits. The Psalter doesn't open with the hallelujahs; it ends with them, after Psalm 88 and Psalm 137 and every how-long. The praise isn't offered instead of the darkness but on the far side of it. It isn't the easy praise of people who have never suffered. It's the praise of a book that told the whole truth first, gave full voice to the pit and the rage and the valley, and then, having hidden nothing, climbed to praise anyway. Papering over would mean starting with the hallelujahs and never mentioning the dark. The Psalter mentions the dark at length, in God's own words, and only then arrives at "Let everything that has breath praise the Lord!" (Psalm 150:6). The climbing is what makes the song true.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you think of worship, do you picture a high moment you keep chasing and mostly missing, or a long road you're actually walking? What would change if you believed the road itself was worship?
sessions.practice: This week, treat worship as a climb. Pray one of the Songs of Ascent each day, Psalms 120 to 134, and let them teach you to worship on the ordinary road. On a day when you feel nothing, lift your eyes anyway with Psalm 121 and turn toward God when there's no high to ride. Then look back over these five weeks and pray the praise you've climbed to. Write down what it means to you that the praise at the end of the book comes after everything, not instead of it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we've wanted the mountaintop and looked down on the road. We've counted only the felt highs as worship and called the long ordinary climb a failure. Teach us what the pilgrims knew: to sing on the dusty uphill days, to lift our eyes to the hills and past them to you who made them, and to worship with a faithful step when nothing is felt. Thank you that your book doesn't skip to the praise but climbs to it, and that after the pit and the rage and the valley it ends in hallelujah. We've walked a hard road together these weeks. Gather it now into praise. And we bless you most of all that while we were climbing toward you, you came all the way down the road to meet us. Let everything that has breath praise the Lord. Amen.
reflection: Do I count only the mountaintop moments as worship? What does that do to the ordinary road where most of my life with God is lived?
Where do I look for help first when I'm in trouble, and what would it take to lift my eyes past it to the God who made it?
Now that I've walked through lament, rage, trust and the long climb, what does it mean to me that the praise comes at the end of the book and not the beginning?
sessions.teaching:
The pilgrims who first sang the Songs of Ascent weren't standing on a mountaintop having a spiritual experience. They were on a long, dusty, uphill road, walking for days toward Jerusalem for one of the festivals, tired and sore and far from home, and these songs were what they sang to keep going. That's the first thing to know about Psalms 120 to 134, the fifteen psalms titled "A Song of Ascents." They're walking songs. Jerusalem sits high in the hills, so every approach to it is a climb, and the title itself pictures worship as a repeated going up, not a summit you reach once and stay on.

So this last session comes to the question the whole study has been building toward: what is worship for? The Songs of Ascent give an answer that surprises us. Worship isn't an escape from ordinary life. It's ordinary life lifting its eyes.

Watch how the collection moves, because it moves like a real road. Psalm 120 starts in trouble: "In my distress I called to the Lord, and he answered me" (Psalm 120:1). The singer lives far away, among people who hate peace (Psalm 120:6). That's where a pilgrimage starts, in the ordinary trouble of a life away from home. Then Psalm 121 asks the traveler's question: "I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?" For an ancient traveler the hills weren't scenery. They were where danger lay. To lift your eyes to them was to look straight at the threat, and the psalm looks past it to the one who made the hills: "My help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth" (Psalm 121:2).

From there the collection climbs and gathers things as it goes. There's the gladness of going up together: "I was glad when they said to me, 'Let us go to the house of the Lord!'" (Psalm 122:1). There's rescue in Psalm 124, and a cry of repentance in Psalm 130: "Out of the depths I cry to you, O Lord!" (Psalm 130:1). There's the stilled soul of Psalm 131: "I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother" (Psalm 131:2). And finally the pilgrims arrive, and the collection ends in Psalm 134 with the servants "who stand by night in the house of the Lord" lifting their hands to bless him (Psalm 134:1-2). It's a whole pilgrimage, from distress in a far country to blessing in God's house, and it's sung on the road the entire way.

Now take the strong case for the mountaintop, because it's a real hunger and I won't sneer at it. It says worship is supposed to be the intense experience, the moment God's nearness feels almost tangible, and that a faith without those moments has become routine. There's truth in that. The high moments are real, they're gifts, God isn't against them, and someone who has never felt his nearness is right to long for it.

But look at the assumption underneath, because it can quietly wreck a life of faith. The assumption is that only the felt highs count as worship. If you believe that, you'll fall silent for the long stretches between the peaks, which is most of a life. The pilgrims knew better. They sang on the road, on the dusty day when nothing was felt, and that singing was worship, the deliberate turning of the heart toward God on an ordinary climb. Most of any real walk with God is that road. These psalms teach us to count the faithful ordinary step as worship and to receive the mountaintop, when it comes, as a gift rather than a wage.

And here's the turn that gathers the whole study. Where does the Psalter end? Not where it began. It doesn't open with the hallelujahs; it closes with them, five psalms of praise ending in "Let everything that has breath praise the Lord!" (Psalm 150:6). That final praise isn't naive. It isn't the easy praise of people who have never suffered. It comes after Psalm 88 and its darkness, after Psalm 137 and its rage, after all the how-longs and valleys, and it has passed through every one of them and come out singing. That's the pattern of the whole book, and it's the pattern of a truthful life with God. We don't skip to the praise. We climb to it. A praise that hadn't been through the pit wouldn't be worth much.

And the last word isn't even about our climbing. While the pilgrim sings his way up toward the house of God, the God he's climbing toward has already come down the road to meet him. He came all the way down, into the pit and the valley and the forsakenness of Psalm 22, and he died praying the Psalms. The long ascent is answered by a longer descent, his. The prayers we were afraid to pray turn out to have been prayed first, and finished, by him.

scriptureStudy.note: "In my distress I called to the Lord, and he answered me." The pilgrim songs begin in trouble and far from home. The climb toward God starts from the ordinary distress of life, not from a summit already reached.

"I lift up my eyes to the hills. ... My help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." The traveler looks past the hills, where danger lay, to their Maker. Worship lifts the eyes from the threat to the God above it.
"I was glad when they said to me, 'Let us go to the house of the Lord!'" The joy is in going up together. These songs were sung by a people climbing side by side, not by solitary seekers.

"Out of the depths I cry to you, O Lord! O Lord, hear my voice!" Even the pilgrimage songs include a cry from the depths. The road to God's house still passes through the pit, and repentance is part of the climb.

"But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother." Near the top of the climb the psalmist stills his own striving. The road leads not to spiritual achievement but to a child's rest in God.

"Come, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand by night in the house of the Lord! Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the Lord!" The Songs of Ascent end in the temple at night. The whole climb is gathered into blessing God in the dark.

"Let everything that has breath praise the Lord! Praise the Lord!" The Psalter ends in praise, but it's praise reached at the end of the whole book, after the lament and the pit. It's the top of a long climb.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look at the Psalter as one book. Scholars have long noticed that it's arranged in five books, often compared to the five books of Moses, and that it's edited with care. It opens with delight in God's law (Psalm 1) and the enthroned king (Psalm 2), runs through a long middle heavy with lament, and ends in sustained praise (Psalms 146 to 150). Ask the group what it means that this order is itself a kind of teaching, and that the inspired hymnbook doesn't begin where an anxious modern worshiper would like to begin.

Bonhoeffer, in Psalms: The Prayer Book of the Bible, argued that the Psalms are finally the prayers of Christ, so that the church praying them prays with and in her Lord. Read the Songs of Ascent that way. Jesus himself went up to Jerusalem for the festivals (Luke 2:41-42; John 7:10), and he went up the last time knowing what waited there (Luke 18:31).

C. S. Lewis's point about praise belongs here too. If praise completes our enjoyment, then the run of hallelujahs at the end of the Psalter isn't tedious repetition. It's joy that has finally found its object and can't stop saying so.

Then the pastoral question that gathers the study. What does it do to a congregation to be handed only the summit and never the climb? A church that sings only mountaintop songs produces worshipers who feel like failures on ordinary days and frauds in the valley. A church that learns to sing on the uphill road produces people who can keep walking toward God through anything, because they were taught that the walking is worship.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group has quietly concluded, over five weeks, that her faith is second-rate. She almost never feels the emotional highs others describe. For years, worship for her has meant being there and doing the next faithful thing without much feeling. As the session describes worship as a long climb, she's near tears, unsure whether to feel relieved or exposed.

Be tender here. She's been carrying a false verdict on herself for a long time. Don't dismiss the mountaintop, because feeling God near is a real gift and her longing for it isn't wrong.

But say plainly what the Songs of Ascent teach. The pilgrims sang on the road, not the summit. The faithful step taken when nothing is felt isn't lesser worship; it's the substance of it. Her long, quiet obedience isn't second-rate faith. It's exactly the kind of worship these songs were written for. Help her see that she's been measuring her whole life by the peaks and missing that she's been climbing faithfully all along. Let her hear, perhaps for the first time, that the God she's been walking toward without much feeling has been walking with her the whole way. Then ask the group where else they've judged their faith by the wrong measure.

memoryVerse.text: I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come? My help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

leaderPrimer:
The particular danger of a study on the Psalms is that it turns into a literature seminar, a room admiring the poetry and never once praying it. Refuse that from the first night. The Psalms are a prayer book to be prayed, and this study has failed if a group finishes it able to discuss lament and still unable to lament. So make the room a place where people actually pray, out loud and in their own words, the prayers the Psalms give them permission to pray.

Set the ground rules early. What's said here stays here, and nobody is here to correct anyone else's grief, anger or doubt, because the Psalter doesn't correct them either; it gives them words. A lot of what matters will happen in silence, in someone realizing they've been praying with a mask on and quietly taking it off before God. Make room for that silence instead of asking for confessions around the circle.

Two sessions carry particular weight, so prepare for them. Session two sits with Psalm 88, the psalm that never resolves. In almost any room someone is living in that psalm right now, and the worst thing you can do is hurry them toward a happy ending the psalm itself refuses. Let the weight sit. Session three faces the cursing psalms, and someone in the room may be a survivor of real evil who has been shamed for their rage. Do not, under any circumstances, meet a disclosure of abuse or trauma with a quick command to forgive. Know a counselor before you begin, keep a path to real help visible, believe people when they tell you what was done to them, and make a private way to reach you. Help information is printed with this guide, and Find Help on the site lists more; know where it is before the first night.

Go in as a fellow beginner who is still learning to pray these prayers. If you present yourself as a master of prayer, the room will perform prayer back at you and nothing will move. Five weeks won't turn anyone into a saint. But they can hand a room the prayer book the church has always had, and teach ordinary people that all of themselves, the praise and the grief and the fury and the doubt, is welcome before God.

faq.q: Is this study going to be a poetry class, or does it actually help me pray?
faq.a: It's built to help you pray. The Psalms are the church's prayer book, and the point of this study is to hand them back to you as words you can actually use, in praise and in protest, in thanksgiving and in the pit. Every session ends in prayer, and each week's practice puts a psalm in your mouth to pray as your own. You'll learn some history and some structure, because knowing what a psalm is doing helps you pray it. But the aim is that you finish praying more truthfully than you started.

faq.q: I struggle with doubt and dark feelings. Will this study make me feel like a bad Christian?
faq.a: No. Lament is the most common kind of psalm in the Psalter, and this study takes that seriously: grief and doubt turned toward God are one of the ways faith speaks. Session two sits with Psalm 13 and Psalm 88, the psalm that ends in darkness, and the point is that God put a prayer for even that place in the Bible. You won't be told to cheer up or have more faith. If your darkness is heavy right now, tell your leader, and use the help information printed with this guide or Find Help on the site.

faq.q: What about the violent psalms, the ones that ask God to hurt people? How can those be in the Bible?
faq.a: Session three faces them instead of skipping them. Psalm 137 ends with a blessing on whoever dashes an enemy's infants against the rock, and the study admits that and asks what it's doing in the prayer book. The answer starts with a distinction: voicing rage to God isn't the same as acting on it. The psalm is the prayer of real victims of a real atrocity, and it doesn't pick up a sword. It hands the vengeance to God, which is the seed of Paul's command to leave vengeance to him (Romans 12:19). The study traces how these prayers point to the cross, it handles the rage with care for anyone carrying real trauma, and it never presents the curse as something to imitate.

faq.q: What's the difference between lament and just complaining or being ungrateful?
faq.a: Direction. Grumbling talks about God behind his back and drifts away from him. Lament brings the same pain to God's face and keeps speaking to him, even in protest. Psalm 13 accuses God of forgetting and hiding, but it says so to God, and it ends in trust reached through the complaint. So lament isn't the opposite of faith or gratitude; it's often the road to them. The alternative to lament usually isn't calm trust. It's silence and quietly leaving.

faq.q: Does the study just tell suffering people to be more thankful?
faq.a: No, and it's careful here. Session four names the real danger of using gratitude to silence grief. Psalm 103 doesn't paste thanks over pain; it's a man telling his own forgetful soul to remember specific mercies, alongside the grief and not instead of it. And Psalm 23 walks straight through the valley of the shadow of death, so its trust is earned on the far side of suffering. The study also warns leaders not to hand the psalms of trust to someone still in the valley as if they were a requirement.

faq.q: I don't feel emotional in worship the way others seem to. Is something wrong with my faith?
faq.a: Session five was written partly for you. The Songs of Ascent were sung by ordinary pilgrims on a long uphill road, not on a mountaintop, and they picture worship as a repeated climb. A faith that counts only the emotional highs will judge the ordinary road a failure, but the pilgrims sang on exactly that road. A faithful step taken when nothing is felt isn't lesser worship. Your long, quiet obedience is the kind of worship these psalms were written for.

faq.q: Why does the study spend so much time on the hard psalms instead of the encouraging ones?
faq.a: Because the hard psalms are a large part of the book, and many churches have quietly left them out. A people that prays only the bright psalms teaches itself that half its inner life isn't welcome before God. The study doesn't neglect encouragement: session four is about trust and thanksgiving, and session five ends in praise. But the praise at the end of the Psalter is reached by going through the lament in the middle, and it means more because nothing was hidden first.

faq.q: Do I need to know the Bible well to lead or join this study?
faq.a: No. It was written for ordinary leaders. Every discussion question has notes on what's behind it, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument. You don't need the historical background of each psalm, because the guide gives you what you need, and you don't need to have your own prayer life figured out. A leader who admits they're still learning to pray will lead better than one who performs mastery.

faq.q: Is it really okay to bring anger at God into my prayers?
faq.a: The Psalms say yes, again and again. Psalm 13 accuses God of forgetting, Psalm 88 says he has caused the darkness, Psalm 22 cries out that he has forsaken the one praying, and all of it is Scripture. The key is that the anger is brought to God rather than carried away from him. Anger handed to him is anger you're no longer carrying alone. What the study won't tell you is that mature faith means hiding your anger behind a brave face.

faq.q: How does this study connect to Jesus, or is it only about the Old Testament?
faq.a: Jesus is at the center. The risen Christ named the Psalms as one of the parts of Scripture that speak of him (Luke 24:44), and he prayed them himself, crying out with Psalm 22 on the cross and committing his spirit with the words of Psalm 31 as he died (Luke 23:46). The study reads lament in the light of a Lord who lamented, the cursing psalms in the light of the cross, and the Songs of Ascent in the light of a Christ who came down the road to meet us. Bonhoeffer called the Psalms the prayers of Christ, which the church is drawn into.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't religion just teaching people to talk themselves into feeling better?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the Psalms are a good place to test it. They're about the least sentimental religious writing you'll find. They give full voice to despair that doesn't lift, rage at real atrocity and doubt that accuses God to his face, and they keep a prayer that ends in darkness as Scripture. Whatever that is, it isn't positive thinking. You don't have to believe what Christians believe to notice that a prayer book containing Psalm 88 isn't in the business of pretending, and to wonder what kind of God would want those prayers prayed.

timeline.event: David, the shepherd who became king, writes psalms of praise, lament and trust. Seventy-three psalms carry his name in their titles, among them Psalm 23.

Solomon's temple stands in Jerusalem, and Israel's families go up to it for the festivals (Deuteronomy 16:16). The Songs of Ascent, Psalms 120 to 134, were sung on that road, though when each was written is uncertain.
Babylon burns Jerusalem, destroys the temple and carries the survivors into exile. Psalm 137 is the prayer of those exiles by the rivers of Babylon.

After the return from exile, the Psalter is gathered and edited over time into five books, moving from delight in God's law in Psalm 1, through a long middle of lament, to the praise of the closing psalms.
The Psalms are translated into Greek as part of the Septuagint, the form in which many of the earliest Christians first read and quoted them.
Jesus prays the Psalms at the cross, crying out with Psalm 22, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" and committing his spirit with the words of Psalm 31.
Athanasius of Alexandria writes his Letter to Marcellinus on the Psalms, observing that in this book the reader finds words he can speak as his own.
Augustine preaches and writes his Expositions of the Psalms, covering the whole Psalter and reading it as the voice of Christ and his body, the church.
Martin Luther, in his preface to the Psalter, calls the book a little Bible, because it gathers the whole of Scripture into one book of prayer.
John Calvin publishes his Commentary on the Psalms. In its preface he calls the book "An Anatomy of all the Parts of the Soul," because every feeling a person can have is pictured in it.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who had trained pastors for the Confessing Church under the Nazi regime, publishes Psalms: The Prayer Book of the Bible, arguing that we learn to pray by praying the words God has given.
C. S. Lewis publishes Reflections on the Psalms, refusing to excuse the hard psalms and yet finding in them a seriousness about God, suffering and evil that gentler religion lacks.

Walter Brueggemann's The Message of the Psalms describes the pattern of orientation, disorientation and new orientation: psalms for a settled life, for a life come apart, and for the surprised trust on the far side.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. It takes some courage to learn to pray truthfully in front of other people. Before we start, three things. First, the Psalms aren't poems we're here to admire; they're a prayer book we're here to pray. So we'll pray out loud in this room, in our own words, and nobody has to do it well. Second, what's said here stays here, and nobody is going to correct anyone else's grief or doubt or anger, because the Psalms don't correct them either. They give them words. Third, we're all beginners at this, me included. One more thing that matters, and I mean it. If anyone here is carrying a darkness that has not lifted, or a rage from a real wrong done to you, this study is built to make room for exactly that, and I am available to talk privately and to help. Tonight we're praying our way through ________. Let me read our key psalm, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what these psalms say. Now let's pray them, off the page and into the lives each of us walked in with, because a study of the prayer book that never turns into prayer has missed the point.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there. If it doesn't feel resolved, that's all right; the Psalms don't resolve everything either. Take the weight of this home instead of setting it down at the door. Pray the psalm this week, out loud, as your own words, and sit with the reflection questions. Come back ready to be truthful, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this conversation, and remember, my door is open if any of you needs it.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about honesty and praying out loud, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly, praying Psalm 62 together.
Week 2: Session 1, The Prayer Book We Were Handed, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, How Long, O Lord, with extended time on Psalm 13 and the turn it makes.
Week 4: Session 2 continued, sitting honestly with Psalm 88, the psalm that does not resolve, with private availability for anyone in that place.
Week 5: Session 3, By the Waters of Babylon, the imprecatory psalms named plainly, with care taken for anyone carrying real trauma.
Week 6: Session 4, The Lord Is My Shepherd, trust and thanksgiving through the valley.
Week 7: Session 5, I Lift Up My Eyes, the Songs of Ascent and the long climb.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, pray your way through the movement of the whole Psalter from lament to praise, and close in the gospel of the God who prayed the honest prayers first.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the Psalter as prayer book and the complaint God invites, including Psalm 88 with care.
Week 2: Session 3, By the Waters of Babylon, the imprecatory psalms named plainly, with care taken for the room.
Week 3: Session 4, The Lord Is My Shepherd, trust and thanksgiving that are earned.
Week 4: Session 5, I Lift Up My Eyes, the Songs of Ascent, plus a short integration close praying the movement of the whole Psalter into praise.

bibliography.title: Psalms: The Prayer Book of the Bible
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Published in 1940. The theological spine of the study: we learn to pray by praying the words God has given, and the Psalms are finally the prayers of Christ, which the church is drawn into. Behind sessions 1, 3 and 5.

bibliography.title: Reflections on the Psalms
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Published in 1958. A literary reader who refuses to excuse the hard psalms, wrestles openly with the cursing psalms, and writes well on praise as the completion of enjoyment. Behind sessions 3, 4 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Message of the Psalms: A Theological Commentary
bibliography.author: Walter Brueggemann
bibliography.note: Published in 1984. The source of the pattern of orientation, disorientation and new orientation that runs through sessions 2 and 4.

bibliography.title: Praying the Psalms: Engaging Scripture and the Life of the Spirit
bibliography.author: Walter Brueggemann
bibliography.note: A shorter book on how the Psalms teach bold, truthful prayer, lament and complaint included. Background for sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: Letter to Marcellinus
bibliography.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
bibliography.note: A fourth-century letter on how to pray the Psalms, observing that the reader finds in them words he can speak as his own. Mentioned in session 1 and the timeline. Short enough to read whole.

bibliography.title: Commentary on the Book of Psalms
bibliography.author: John Calvin
bibliography.note: Published in 1557. Its preface calls the book "An Anatomy of all the Parts of the Soul." Mentioned in session 1 and the timeline.

bibliography.title: Expositions of the Psalms
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Augustine's sermons and notes on the whole Psalter, reading it as the voice of Christ and his body, the church. Very long; read selectively.

bibliography.title: Open and Unafraid: The Psalms as a Guide to Life
bibliography.author: W. David O. Taylor
bibliography.note: A pastoral guide to praying the Psalms across the whole range of human feeling, from anger and sadness to joy. An accessible companion for group members.

bibliography.title: Prophetic Lament: A Call for Justice in Troubled Times
bibliography.author: Soong-Chan Rah
bibliography.note: Published in 2015. On the church's loss of lament and the cost of worship that sings only triumph. Background for session 2.

bibliography.title: The Case for the Psalms: Why They Are Essential
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Published in 2013. An accessible argument that the Psalms shape a Christian's sense of time, space and God, and that the church is poorer for neglecting them. Background for session 1.

bibliography.title: The Book of Psalms
bibliography.author: the psalmists of Israel
bibliography.note: The prayer book at the heart of the whole study, to be read, prayed and sung, not only discussed.

furtherReading: Psalms: The Prayer Book of the Bible, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for the fuller case that the Psalms are a school of prayer and finally the prayers of Christ.
Reflections on the Psalms, C. S. Lewis, for a companion who doesn't pretend the hard psalms are easy and still finds their rawness truer than polite religion.
The Message of the Psalms, Walter Brueggemann, for the fuller account of orientation, disorientation and new orientation behind sessions 2 and 4.
Open and Unafraid, W. David O. Taylor, for group members who want a warm, readable guide to praying the whole range of the Psalms.
The Book of Psalms itself, prayed slowly and out loud, a psalm a day, for anyone willing to let it teach them to pray.

glossary.definition: The Book of Psalms: a hundred and fifty prayers and songs that were the prayer book of Israel and then of the church, gathered into five books and moving from meditation through lament to praise.
A prayer that brings pain, grief and complaint to God rather than away from him, and stays turned toward him even in protest. The most common kind of psalm.

A psalm that calls down God's judgment on enemies, such as Psalm 137 or Psalm 69. The study reads these as rage handed over to God rather than vengeance endorsed, and traces how they point to the cross.
Psalms 120 to 134, fifteen psalms titled "A Song of Ascents," sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the festivals. They picture worship as a long, repeated climb.
Brueggemann's term for psalms of a settled, ordered life, where the world makes sense and God is reliably good, such as many of the wisdom and creation psalms.
Brueggemann's term for psalms of a life come apart: the laments and complaints prayed when the settled world has broken and the bright psalms no longer fit.

Brueggemann's term for the surprised trust reached on the far side of disorientation. It isn't the old confidence restored but a deeper trust formed in the valley, as in the psalms of thanksgiving and Psalm 23.

The ESV's usual rendering of the Hebrew hesed: God's faithful, covenant love toward a people who haven't earned it. It's named again and again as the ground of the psalmist's trust, especially in Psalm 103.
A Hebrew word that appears often in the Psalms. Its exact meaning is uncertain; it's probably a musical or liturgical direction, and many take it as a pause, a place to stop before praying on.
The move at the heart of the cursing psalms: the psalmist brings his rage to God and leaves the repaying with him instead of taking it himself. Paul builds on it in Romans 12:19.
Bonhoeffer's description of the Psalms: Christ prayed them in his life and death, so the church praying them prays with and in her Lord, even the psalms she can't yet fully mean.
In the Psalter, not the cheer of people who have never suffered but the song reached at the end of the book, after the lament and the pit and the valley.
The festival climb up to Jerusalem that gave rise to the Songs of Ascent, and a picture of the life of worship as a long road walked toward God, mostly ordinary and uphill.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Most of us were taught how to praise God and never taught what to do with grief, doubt or rage. The Psalms were. This five-session study hands back the church's own prayer book, where God teaches his people to speak to him about the whole of their lives. It takes in the Psalter as a school of prayer, the lament God invites, the hard words of the cursing psalms and what to do with real anger, the trust and thanksgiving earned on the far side of the valley, and the long climb of worship in the Songs of Ascent. It's truthful about the dark and careful with real pain, and anyone can lead it with little preparation. Come honest, not finished.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on the Psalms, and it isn't a poetry class. It's a school of prayer. The Psalms are the prayer book God gave his people, and they hold far more than praise. They hold the lament, the doubt and even the rage most churches quietly skip. This study hands the whole book back, teaches us to bring God the parts of our lives we thought were unwelcome, and takes care with anyone carrying real darkness or real hurt. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: You were probably taught how to praise God. Were you ever taught what to do with grief, doubt or rage? The Psalms were. A five-session study on the church's own prayer book: the lament God invites, the prayers we were afraid to pray, trust earned through the valley, and the long climb of worship. Come honest, not finished.
quoteCards: We don't clean ourselves up to pray. We bring what's actually in us to the one who can do something with it.
Many of us were taught a hundred ways to praise and not one way to grieve toward God.
God put a prayer with no happy ending in the prayer book on purpose. There's a psalm for even this.
The opposite of lament isn't calm trust. The opposite of lament is leaving.
The psalmist doesn't pick up a sword. He hands the vengeance to God.
Psalm 23 isn't a lullaby. It walks straight through the valley of the shadow of death.
We don't skip to the praise. We climb to it.
The prayers we were afraid to pray turn out to have been prayed first, and finished, by him.
